The Arizona State Board of Accountancy consists of five certified public accountants (CPAs) and two public members, all of whom are  residents of the state and are appointed by the Governor. The Board and its committees also receive and investigate complaints, take  enforcement action against licensees for violation of statutes and regulations, monitor compliance with continuing education requirements, and review the work product of CPAs to ensure adherence to professional standards through the Board's peer review program.

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Ensure Health Insurance Trust Fund Solvency

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $447.6 million in one-time funding and $100 million in ongoing funding for agency premium  increases to the Health Insurance Trust Fund (HITF).

The increase includes a one-time FY 2027 General Fund impact of $172.8 million and an ongoing FY 2027 General Fund impact of $100  million.

The Fund supports the State's self-insured medical, pharmacy, and dental insurance for State employees.

The Executive Budget contemplates that, by FY 2029, the State will fund agency health premiums entirely on an ongoing basis. This  change in practice protects the State against the need for larger and larger one-time investments to offset the growing cost of healthcare.

A detailed breakdown of the agency and fund impact from this premium increase is included in the Statewide Adjustments section of the  Executive Budget.

Risk Management Claims & Premiums

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $6.6 million in ongoing funding to address renewed actuarial assumptions regarding the  State’s risk exposure, potential claims, and claims-related expenditures in FY 2027.

Monies from the Risk Management Revolving Fund are used to support administrative and operational expenses, risk management  premium costs, and claims arising from personal injury, loss, and other harm.

Nonprofit Local Education Agency Support

Administration, Department of

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.0 million in one-time funding to award a grant to a non-profit entity with experience in  youth development activities to provide student success coaches (SSCs) to public schools.

SSCs collaborate with school principals and teachers to reduce early-warning indicators, such as low attendance and course failure. In  other states, SSCs have demonstrated evidence of impact on students.

Evaluations have found that schools that partner with SSCs are up to two to three times more likely to improve English and math assessment scores, and that the SSC model’s focus on personalized learning and developmental relationships builds student engagement and  connection to school, which has the potential to reduce the number of students who are off-track to high school graduation.

State Employee Professional Development Funding

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.0 million in one-time funding for State employee professional development.

After providing funding for 740 placements in FY 2026, all seats were filled within one month of the initial launch. The success of this  program supports employee engagement and improves the efficacy of the workforce in one of the most cost-effective available methods  to retain staff.

This second year of one-time investment enables the State to preserve its partnership with State universities to provide, for State  employees seeking to upskill or gain new degrees or certifications, job training and access to new job-relevant skills and courses.

Enterprise Resource Planning Division Development

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $7.5 million in ongoing funding and 18 FTE positions to establish the Department of  Administration Enterprise Resource Planning Division (ADOA-ERP).

Administration, Department of

Once initial development concludes in FY 2026, the funding will enable ADOA to meet contractual obligations, retain expertise, comply  with State and federal law, and address security risks associated with the new AZ360 human resources and accounting platform.

AHCCCS

Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System

Founded in 1982, the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS) is Arizona's Medicaid program, a federal health care  program jointly funded by the federal and state governments for individuals and families who qualify based on income level. Built on principles of competition and choice, AHCCCS operates under an integrated care model for its American Indian Health program (fee-forservice) and contracted managed care organizations (MCOs) (health plans) to coordinate and pay for physical and behavioral health  care services delivered by more than 100,000 health care providers to approximately 2 million Arizonans. AHCCCS also serves as the  state behavioral health authority, which includes the administration of grant funding from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health  Services Administration (SAMHSA) and other sources. Arizona receives national recognition for its innovative approach to behavioral  health crisis services. For example, Arizona operates 24/7 crisis call centers to respond to people in need (regardless of insurance  coverage) and dispatch mobile crisis teams.

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

H.R. 1 Mitigation

The Executive Budget includes an increase  of $11.5 million in one-time funding to AHCCCS to help mitigate the impacts of H.R. 1 on  health care recipients and facilities.

H.R. 1 is expected to cause tens of thousands of individuals in Arizona to lose Medicaid coverage. This will increase strain on those individuals’ health and finances as well as straining the overall healthcare system as hospital emergency departments see increased use  with less federal funding. Arizona hospitals will receive $5.2 Billion less federal funding from FY 2029 through FY 2033 from the provider  assessment cap reduction alone.

To help mitigate the worst impacts on individuals and healthcare providers, the Executive Budget funds the following initiatives:

Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System

- $4.3 million for a Critical Access Hospital supplemental funding pool. This will help hospitals in rural areas remain solvent in the face of  massive declines in federal revenue due to H.R. 1.

- $4.0 million for 988 hotline costs for the State's crisis behavioral health services network. This will help ensure every call is answered,  whether a caller is a Medicaid member or not.

- $2.2 million to help individuals navigate the new healthcare insurance and social service program environment. This will provide assistance to those affected by Medicaid changes as well as other changes to the healthcare insurance landscape (i.e. less access to Affordable Care Act marketplace plans).

- $1.0 million to support crisis resource centers to guide Arizonans to housing, heat relief, utility assistance, crisis intervention, and other  resources. This will help address a wide range of areas in which individuals are currently experiencing hardship, while connecting more  people to resources to ease the strain of losing Medicaid.

- The Executive Budget also continues funding the AZ REACH program. Details and appropriations for this item can be found in the  University of Arizona Health Sciences Center section.

Cost Containment Data Analytics

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $600,000 in ongoing funding for 7.0 additional FTE positions to establish a data analytics  cost containment team.

The new team will utilize new functionality enabled by AHCCCS' new Medicaid Enterprise IT System as well as artificial intelligence and  advanced data techniques to crack down on fraudulent billing codes. This investment builds upon the Executive's prior fraud, waste, and  abuse prevention efforts in response to the Sober Living Home crisis.

Office of Inspector General

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $365,000 in ongoing funding for an increase of 7.0 FTE positions in AHCCCS' Office of  Inspector General.

Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System

The additional positions will assist with investigation, enforcement, and prosecution of bad actors and serve as a deterrent to prevent  fraudulent activity within the State's Medicaid program. This investment builds upon the Executive's prior fraud, waste, and abuse  prevention efforts in response to the Sober Living Home crisis.

MES Modernization

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $112.8 million in one-time funding for the sixth of seven funding phases of replacing the  AHCCCS mainframe IT system. Funding is provided by $15.2 million from the General Fund and $97.5 million in matching federal funds.

The funding continues a vital multi-year replacement project, which is scheduled to be completed by the end of FY 2028. The current  legacy system is over 40 years old and operates on an outdated coding language. A system outage would impact all major AHCCCS  functions, from case management to provider payments.

Transfers and appropriations for this project appear in the Statewide and Large Automation Projects section of the Executive Budget.

External Legal Services

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.4 million in one-time funding to address an increase in outside legal costs.

Since FY 2023, AHCCCS has incurred higher-than-normal legal costs in connection with an increase in legal inquiries regarding the  agency's response to the Sober Living Home crisis.

This investment continues one-time funding provided in FY 2026.

Arizona – Perinatal Access Line (A-PAL)

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.2 million in ongoing funding to continue operations of the Arizona Perinatal Access Line  (A-PAL).

A-PAL provides a critical resource to rural and underserved areas that lack mental health providers for pre- and post-natal health care.

A-PAL functions as a provider hotline hosted at the University of Arizona. Healthcare providers can call for best practices and recommendations on care for pre- and post-natal health care.

Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $5.3 million in ongoing funding to implement the federally approved Justice Reentry  services waiver.

The Justice Reentry program will allow Medicaid to provide pre-release services to incarcerated persons 90 days before release.  Covered services include case management, peer support services, medication assisted treatment, medical practitioner visits, and a 30day supply of prescribed medicine upon release.

These services are expected to reduce recidivism rates and will offset existing costs at the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation, and Reentry.

H.R. 1 Impacts on Medicaid The Executive Budget includes an increase of $14.4 million in one-time funding to address increased costs due to H.R. 1 provisions  impacting the Department’s administration of the Medicaid program. Medicaid is a joint state and federal program that provides health  insurance to eligible low-income households and plays a key role in providing access to health care services. H.R. 1 results in three major changes that will increase the administrative burden to operate Medicaid, for both members and AHCCCS.  Those include (1) work requirements; (2) doubles the frequency of eligibility redeterminations; and (3) imposes extensive requirements  on states to verify member addresses. Work Requirements H.R. 1 implements a new requirement that single adults eligible for Medicaid in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expansion population  complete 80 hours a month of work, community service, education, or job training activities.

AHCCCS estimates that as many as 190,000 members who would otherwise be eligible could lose coverage due to these new work  requirements. This will result in individuals forgoing care, utilizing hospital emergency departments more often, and taking on medical  debt. This will reduce funding provided to the healthcare system, place further strain on already stretched hospital emergency departments, and increase hospitals’ uncompensated care burden. 6 Month Eligibility Redeterminations H.R. 1 increases the frequency with which states must recheck Medicaid eligibility for members who are single adults eligible under the  ACA expansion population. Instead of once a year, states must perform the eligibility redetermination process every 6 months for these  members. For these members, this means the State will have to double the administrative work to check eligibility each year, increasing  time spent by both Medicaid recipients and AHCCCS staff by millions of hours per year.  AHCCCS estimates that between 35,000 and 50,000 members who would otherwise be eligible could lose coverage due to more  frequent eligibility redeterminations. This will result in individuals forgoing care, utilizing hospital emergency departments more often, and  taking on medical debt. This will reduce funding provided to the healthcare system, place further strain on already stretched hospital  emergency departments, and increase hospitals’ uncompensated care burden. Verifying Members Addresses H.R. 1 alters current processes for verifying member addresses. Prior to H.R. 1, states verified member addresses at the point of initial  application as well as by return mail for certain communications like renewals and information requests. H.R. 1 will result in states having  to further verify addresses beyond the use of return mail from additional data sources to be identified by the federal government.

Department of Child Safety

Child Safety, Department of

The Department of Child Safety (DCS) provides child abuse and neglect investigations; child safety and risk assessments; family  support, preservation and reunification services, kinship care services and family foster care; prevention services to promote the safety,  permanence and well-being of children with birth, kinship, foster, legal guardianship and adoptive families; adoption promotion and  support services; and health care services for children in out-of-home care. DCS also offers extended foster care services and supports  for youth exiting care from age 18-21.

The primary purpose of DCS is to protect children. To achieve this purpose, DCS seeks to accomplish the following in equal priority: (a)  investigate reports of child abuse and neglect; (b) assess, promote and support the safety of a child in a safe and stable family or other  appropriate placement; (c) work cooperatively with law enforcement regarding reports that include criminal conduct allegations; and (d)  without compromising child safety, coordinate services to achieve permanency on behalf of the child, strengthen the family, and provide  prevention, intervention, and treatment for abuse and neglected children.

Link to the AGENCY’S WEBSITE:    https://dcs.az.gov/

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Child Safety Information System

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $16.0 million in ongoing funding to support operational costs of Guardian, the State’s child  safety information system.

The Guardian system is essential in supporting the Department’s ability to deliver timely and effective services to Arizona’s children and  families. Since implementation, the Department has relied on a variety of one-time sources to maintain the system as federally required.  Those sources are no longer available.

Child Safety, Department of

Guardian replaced the 24-year-old CHILDS system in FY 2021. It is a cloud-based system that was designed to meet Arizona’s specific  needs. The system has made the Department more efficient, provided ease of use by caseworkers, and created robust reporting for  inter-agency communication. The system covers all aspects of the Department’s operations and supports tens of millions of critical operational interactions annually through caseworker management, family interactions, court interactions, provider network management,  school interactions, Medicaid interactions, and much more.

Placeholder - Children & Family Supports Contracts

The Executive Budget includes a placeholder for additional funding for the following contracts:

- Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP)

- Behavioral Health (BH)

- Non-Medical Transportation (NMT)

- Substance Abuse Service

- Family Connections (FC)

- Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children (ICPC)

- Child Specific Recruitment (CSR)

Each of these contracts are overdue to be rebid. In past years, DCS has obtained one-year extensions to the current contracts, but that  is no longer sustainable for the provider network.

DCS will begin the Request for Proposal (RFP) process in early 2026. The Executive will inform the Legislature of the outcome of the  RFP process.

Executive Budget Baseline Changes

Caseload - Congregate Care

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $36.9 million in ongoing funding to backfill reductions to federal IV-E funding for congregate care expenses and to address increased costs associated with the placement of children with complex needs under the Department’s care.

Pursuant to the federal Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA), a child placed in a group home after October 1, 2020, is not  eligible for federal IV-E funding after 14 days in care. Since FFPSA implementation, the percentage of children in group home placements who are eligible for IV-E funding fell from 48.7% in FY 2021 to 7.2% at the end of FY 2025.

Child Safety, Department of

This funding is a continuation of the one-time funding provided in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget to address the funding gap.

To reduce the growth of the congregate care population while supporting foster families, the family foster care rate was increased on  December 1, 2025 for children aged 6 and older. The initial cost of this change is funded by the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)  monies. The enhanced rate will encourage increased placements in family-like settings and is anticipated to reduce the growth of congregate care placements while improving outcomes for children.

Caseload - Extended Foster Care

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.1 million in ongoing funding for increased caseloads and costs for Extended Foster  Care placements.

Young adults in the care of the Department of Child Safety have the option of voluntarily enrolling in Extended Foster Care until age 21.  This option provides stable housing to help them pursue educational and career goals in preparation for life outside foster care.

The number of individuals seeking Extended Foster Care services is expected to increase from 1,003 to 1,064 in FY 2027. In addition,  the average cost per month for each placement is expected to increase from $2,057 to $2,104.

Extended Foster Care Success Coaching Program

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $10.7 million in one-time funding for the Extended Foster Care Success Coaching  program to support young adults transitioning to adulthood.

The program has experienced immense popularity among eligible young adults, with caseloads growing by over 180% since implementation in FY 2024. In FY 2027, the average number of individuals enrolled in the program is expected to increase by 9%, from 1,340 to  1,460. Participating young adults work with success coach providers and receive life skills training, education assistance, housing assistance, career planning, and other services to support their transition from foster care to adulthood.

Child Safety, Department of

The program shows early success has been experienced, with 95% of young adults having gained essential skills such as completing  educational goals, accessing healthcare services, receiving a driver’s license, and receiving financial literacy training.

FMAP Adjustment

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.9 million in ongoing funding from the General Fund to backfill a reduction in federal  funding due to a 0.53% decrease in the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP). A corresponding decrease of $(1.9) million  from the DCS Expenditure Authority Fund is included to account for the anticipated reduction in federal funding.

This change will impact multiple special line item programs at the Department of Child Safety, including Foster Home Placement,  Extended Foster Care, Out-of-Home Services, Adoption Services, Congregate Care, and Child Care Subsidy.

FMAP changes are driven by a multi-year rolling average of a state’s per capita income compared to all other states. As Arizona’s per  capita income increases relative to other states, its FMAP decreases.

Department of Corrections

Corrections, Department of

The Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation, and Reentry is committed to enhancing public safety throughout Arizona. Our  mission is rooted in the adoption of modern, effective correctional practices and fostering meaningful engagements within the community. With a vision that centers around "Reimagining Corrections," we aim to transform the traditional power and control mentality into one  that prioritizes respect, rapport, and active engagement.

Guided by a set of principles that define our approach, we are dedicated to consistently delivering a perfect effort in all aspects of our  work. Our commitment extends to the transformation of correctional practices, placing emphasis on the development of our staff to  ensure meaningful performance and positive outcomes. We recognize the importance of responsiveness, effective communication, and  responsible service to the public and population we serve.

In our pursuit of excellence, we strive to develop solutions that not only address immediate challenges but also promote systemic wellness. Our focus on transparency, accountability, and humanity underlines every initiative we undertake, ensuring that our actions align  with the highest standards of ethical conduct.

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Health Care Federal Court Injunction

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $118.3 million in one-time funding in FY 2027 and an ongoing advance appropriation of  $108.2 million in FY 2028 to fully implement the Court-Ordered Final Staffing Plan and continue funding prior years’ non-healthcare, onetime funding for injunction-related needs.

Corrections, Department of

After nearly 10 years of litigation, the federal court issued a permanent injunction in April 2023 in the Jensen v. Thornell case. The injunction mandates specific standards that the Department must meet to ensure compliance with constitutional requirements for people  receiving care through the justice system’s health care services. In June 2025, the Court ordered ADCRR to implement the Court Monitors’ Final Staffing Plan, which increases healthcare FTE positions by 615.3. This funding allows the Department to pay the NaphCare  contract at the higher FTE position level ordered by the Final Staffing Plan.

The FY 2025 and FY 2026 Enacted Budgets included $9.5 million and 23.0 FTE positions one-time for mandated injunction-related, nonhealthcare costs, such as pest control and enhanced sanitation. The Executive Budget continues funding for these costs.

The Executive Budget also includes $10.1 million from the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS) Fund beginning in  FY 2028, utilizing the 1115 Waiver to cover the Court-Ordered Final Staffing Plan. Details regarding the funding appear in the agency  detail section for AHCCCS.

Correctional Officer Retention Package

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $23.7 million in ongoing funding to provide 4.0% pay increases for Correctional Officer  series positions.

Without the additional funding Correctional Officer series employees will experience a pay reduction and current positive retention and  recruitment trends may reverse. The Correctional Officer II (COII) vacancy rate has decreased from 16.2% in July to 14.0% in November  2025. COII position vacancies have not been this low since December 2017.

The FY 2026 Enacted Budget included a one-time 4.0% correctional officer stipend for filled FTE positions. This initiative continues that  funding and includes additional funding to cover all 8,701 Correctional Officer FTE positions.

Prison Safety and Body Worn Cameras

Corrections, Department of

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $5.1 million in one-time funding in FY 2027 and advance appropriates $10.1 million onetime in FY 2028 and $15.2 million ongoing in FY 2029 to expand the Department’s body-worn camera (BWC) deployment to reduce  violent incidents at Arizona State prison complexes (ASPCs).

The Department has seen an increase in violence at its prison facilities, including a 450.0% increase in homicides from FY 2021 to FY  2025. In response to this violence, in May 2025 the Department implemented a pilot program for BWCs. The BWCs were deployed in  close custody, maximum custody, mental health, and detention units. Between May 2025 and October 2025, the Department observed a  40.0% decrease in staff assaults with injury, 20.3% decrease in major disciplinary violation resolution time, and 6.8% decrease in use-offorce incidents.

The funding covers a three-year phased expansion of BWCs to all ASPCs, establishes a 30-month replacement and upgrade cycle, and  provides unlimited video footage storage.

Non-Contract Medication Appropriation Increase

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $6.7 million in ongoing funding for the costs associated with treating incarcerated persons  for substance use disorder (SUD) and Hepatitis C (Hep C).

The Department currently funds costs associated with medication-assisted treatment (MAT), medications for opioid use disorder  (MOUD), and Hep C with available monies from opioid settlement agreement payments in the Opioid Remediation Fund (ORF) and  General Fund monies from the Non-Contract Medication special line item. However, the cash balance in the ORF is not anticipated to  fund all allowable costs associated with treating individuals for SUD and Hep C.

The included funding will allow the Department to continue to treat incarcerated individuals for SUD and Hep C. On average, the Department treats 6,000 incarcerated persons with MAT/MOUD each month and 4,755 incarcerated persons for Hep C each month.

Operating and Budgetary Support

Corrections, Department of

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $42.7 million in ongoing funding, a net decrease of $7.7 million ongoing from three of the  Department’s other appropriated funds, and consolidation of the Department’s special line item (SLI) appropriations to support quality  service delivery and practice, resource sustainability, and operational alignment in response to declining Correctional Officer vacancy  rates and routine operating burdens.

Over the past three fiscal years, the Department’s budget has been reduced and supplemented with other fund capacity. The Department’s other funds have become structurally imbalanced due to enacted appropriations, non-appropriated spending needs, and statutory  transfers. Consequently, the Executive Budget adjusts the Department’s General Fund and other fund appropriations with respect to the  anticipated capacity in the fund.

The Department’s vacancy rate among Correctional Officer II (COII) FTE positions has declined to July 2017 levels. Common practice in  recent years has been for the Department to utilize vacancy savings to cover critical operating expenses. Due to decreased vacancies,  the Department can no longer support this practice, and additional funding is needed for the Department to provide the same level of  service and meet contractual obligations.

Additionally, the Executive Budget consolidates the Department’s SLI appropriations to reflect the actual operations of the Department of  Corrections, Rehabilitation, and Reentry. The consolidations are outlined below:

- Operating Lump Sum: The Executive Budget eliminates the Overtime and Compensatory Time SLI, eliminates the Community Corrections SLI, and moves the combined funding of $106.8 million and 184.0 FTE positions to the Department’s operating lump sum.

Corrections, Department of

- Jensen Injunction Compliance SLI: The Executive Budget creates a new Jensen Injunction Compliance SLI, eliminates the Inmate  Health Care Contracted Services SLI, eliminates the Non-Contract Medication SLI, eliminates the Injunction Related IT Upgrades SLI,  and moves the combined funding of $398.4 million from the eliminated SLIs to the new Jensen Injunction Compliance SLI.

The Executive Budget includes proposed Legislative changes to implement the SLI consolidations and increase the fund transfer to the  Building Renewal and Preventative Maintenance Fund. The proposed language can be found in the Executive Budget Legislative  Changes section.

Private Prison Technical Rate Adjustment

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $55.3 million in one-time funding for increased operational costs associated with private  prison contract rate changes.

The contract changes are negotiated per diem, and the funding is needed to support the Department’s anticipated FY 2027 contractual  obligations.

Arizona State Schools for the Deaf and the Blind

Deaf and the Blind, State Schools for the

Arizona State Schools for the Deaf and the Blind (ASDB) was founded in 1912. ASDB provides education and support services to over  2,000 children who are blind, visually impaired, deaf, hard of hearing, or deafblind, from birth to grade 12. ASDB operates two site-based  campuses, three regional cooperatives, and a statewide distance itinerant program.  ASDB also has a birth to age 5 Early Learning  Program made of two components: The first component is the birth to age 3 program in which early childhood teachers go into the homes  of infants and their caretakers. The second component includes the three preschools located at the Phoenix Day School for the Deaf, the  Arizona School for the Deaf, and the Foundation for Blind Children.

ASDB is committed to excellence and innovation in (a) education for all Arizona children who are hard of hearing or deaf or have vision  loss; (b) leadership and service; (c) collaboration with families, school districts, communities, and others; and (d) partnership with other  agencies that will enable children who are hard of hearing or deaf or have vision loss to succeed now and in the future.

The Arizona Early Childhood Development and Health Board seeks to ensure the quality and accessibility of early childhood development and health programs at the community level. A voter-approved initiative, Proposition 203, created the Board, which is commonly  known as “First Things First.”

Housing Acceleration Fund

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.5 million in one-time funding to support the Housing Acceleration Fund.

To amplify this, the Governor has allocated an additional $2.5 million investment of federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) monies in  FY 2026. Agency Budget Summary

Economic Security, Department of

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding H.R. 1 Impacts on SNAP The Executive Budget includes an increase of $48.4 million in one-time funding to address increased costs due to H.R. 1 provisions  impacting the Department’s administration of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). SNAP is a federal program that provides food assistance to eligible low-income households and plays a crucial role in addressing food  insecurity. H.R. 1 results in three major changes to the program: (1) expands work requirements; (2) imposes financial penalties; and (3) increases  states’ share of administrative costs. Expanded Work Requirements H.R. 1 modifies SNAP work requirements, such as increasing the able-bodied adults without dependents (ABAWD) age limit from 54 to  64, removing the “insufficient jobs” option for states to request an ABAWD waiver, and eliminating exemptions for veterans, persons  experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth under the age of 25. These changes are expected to reduce the number of individuals participating in SNAP and, therefore, reduce the total amount of SNAP  benefits issued. Financial Penalties Beginning in federal fiscal year (FFY) 2028, states will be required to cover up to 15% of SNAP benefit issuances, depending on the  state’s payment error rate (PER) in FFY 2025 or FFY 2026. PER measures the accuracy of eligibility and benefit determinations. A state with a payment error rate that is:

- less than 6% results in a match rate of 0%,

- at least 6% but less than 8%, results in a match rate of 5%,

- at least 8% but less than 10%, results in a match rate of 10%, and

- 10% or greater, results in a match rate of 15%.

Economic Security, Department of

Arizona’s PER was 8.8% in FFY 2024, below the national average of 10.9%. If the State’s PER is 8.8% in FFY 2026, the Department  would be required to cover 10% of SNAP benefit issuances, or approximately $195.4 million in State fiscal year (SFY) 2028. However,  the Department's cost share could reach nearly $300 million if the State's PER is above 10%. The Department has already begun efforts to reduce the State’s PER below 6% in FFY 2026. An increase of $16.6 million in one-time  funding is intended to continue the Department's efforts to lower the State’s PER to meet the federal rate of 6%. This includes funding to  fill 146.0 FTE positions. Increases State's Share of Administrative Costs Currently, states cover 50% of administrative costs to implement SNAP. Beginning in FFY 2027, states’ share of administrative costs will  increase to 75%. As FFY 2027 begins on October 1, 2026, this H.R. 1 change will be in effect for only three quarters of SFY 2027. This  equates to an additional cost of $31.8 million. The federal mandates within H.R. 1 place significant administrative burdens on the State and on Arizona taxpayers while providing  approximately $75.0 million in savings to the federal government.  Other investments to address the administrative burden of H.R. 1 can be found in the agency detail sections for the Arizona Health Care  Cost Containment System and Department of Environmental Quality.

Child Care Assistance Program

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $44.8 million in ongoing funding to support the Department's Child Care Assistance  program.

The program provides child care assistance to eligible families that are working or participating in other eligible activities.

Economic Security, Department of

Without reliable access to child care, parents and other caregivers may miss work or leave the workforce altogether. Employers benefit  as the workforce becomes more reliable, strengthening the State's economy. Providing additional support to the Department’s child care  efforts will help ensure that eligible Arizona families have access to affordable, high-quality child care, resulting in a more reliable workforce.

This funding increase will allow the Department to maintain the current 40% quality enhancement rate that helps ensure that high-quality  care is being provided. An average of 18,100 children per month are expected to be served in FY 2027.

If this funding is not maintained, the Department will need to either reduce the quality enhancement rate to nearly 10% or serve, on  average, nearly 3,800 fewer children per month.

SUN Bucks - Summer 2027

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.8 million in one-time funding to support SUN Bucks Summer 2027.

This federal program provides a $120 grocery benefit during the summer months, when children lose access to free or reduced-price  meals. States are required to provide a 50% administrative match to draw down federal monies, with the federal government covering  100% of benefit costs.

SUN Bucks and similar nutrition programs have demonstrated to be effective in reducing food insecurity and lifting millions of children out  of hunger.

Without this investment, approximately 640,000 children are projected to lose access to this grocery benefit and face increased food  insecurity. Additionally, the State will forfeit approximately $78.4 million in federal funding.

Supporting Victims and Survivors of Crime

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $11.5 million in ongoing funding to backfill decreased federal Victims of Crime Act (VOCA)  funding and one-time funding included in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget.

Economic Security, Department of

The national distribution of VOCA funding has decreased in recent years and is not a reliable funding source. VOCA allocations come  from the Crime Victim Fund, for which a large amount of its fund balance is reserved for pending litigation. Congress has also been  reducing the amount of money allowed to be spent from the Fund, thus reducing the annual allocations to states.

The Department utilizes the VOCA funding to support the Adult Protective Services (APS) program. APS receives and investigates  reports of abuse, neglect, and exploitation committed against vulnerable adults. If the allegation meets specific criteria, APS is statutorily  required to open an investigation. In FY 2025, 42,500 allegations of maltreatment were reported to APS.

The additional funding will backfill 124.0 FTE positions, of which 99.0 FTE positions were previously funded with VOCA and 25.0 FTE  positions are related to increased caseloads throughout the years. This funding will help APS maintain an investigator caseload ratio of  1:25 and the quality and timeliness of the investigation process. Alternatively, if funding is not backfilled, the investigator caseload ratio is  expected to increase by a factor of six, while slowing service significantly.

By maintaining an appropriate caseload level, APS is able to address reports more effectively and help ensure the well-being of one of  the state’s most vulnerable populations.

Other investments can be found in the agency detail sections for the Department of Public Safety and the Arizona Criminal Justice  Commission.

Reentry Employment Support

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $3.0 million in ongoing funding to support the Reentry program, including 31.0 FTE positions, by backfilling federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) funding.

Economic Security, Department of

The Reentry program provides services, such as employment referrals and job fairs, to near-release individuals and those on parole.  Reentry services support formerly incarcerated persons' reintegration into the community by removing barriers, including limited employment. The program also serves a pivotal role in supporting the State's efforts toward achieving Reentry 2030 goals, including increasing  the number of individual employed one year after release by 20%.

Between FY 2022 and FY 2025, 5,400 local employers have participated, and over 14,500 job placements have occurred.

The Department has historically utilized WIOA funding to cover costs associated with the Reentry program. The State's WIOA award is  expected to decline by approximately 10% in FY 2027; therefore, the Department is unable to leverage WIOA funding to support this  program.

Without addressing the loss of federal funding, over 7,000 individuals would lose access to these reentry services, hindering the individuals' ability to secure employment while increasing the likelihood of being incarcerated again.

Keeping DDD Members in Home and Community Based Settings

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $17.9 million in one-time funding to continue $14.8 million in one-time funding included in  the FY 2026 Enacted Budget and address an estimated 8% annual growth in the cost of Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD)  members who exceed the Cost Effectiveness Study (CES) threshold.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) requires a client’s Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) costs to be at  or below the cost of an institutional setting. The Cost Effectiveness Study – Client Services special line item funds the cost of members  above the CES threshold.

In FY 2024, CES costs totaled $20.8 million. In FY 2027, CES costs are projected to total $26.2 million. Growth in CES expenditures are  primarily due to DDD members’ increased medical and behavioral complexity.

Economic Security, Department of

This funding is intended to allow DDD members to stay in home and community-based settings rather than institutional settings,  improving the quality of life of members.

A to Z Arizona Portal Implementation

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.5 million in ongoing funding for the continued implementation of the A to Z Arizona  Portal, including 6.0 additional FTE positions. Of this amount, $1.2 million is intended to continue one-time funding included in the FY  2026 Enacted Budget.

This investment is expected to draw down nearly $8.0 million in federal funds.

The Portal enhances the public's online access to services and deploys strengthened security measures to ensure that benefits are  provided efficiently and only to eligible Arizona residents. Safe, effective data-sharing protects public information and removes service  roadblocks.

To date, the Department has integrated two programs into the Portal: the Child Care Assistance Program and the Low Income Home  Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP). As of November 3, 2025, 57% of Child Care Assistance Program applicants are self-served  online.

This funding will ensure the Portal's continued success and allow for continued enhanced efforts to prevent fraud, waste, and abuse.

Increased Mainframe Contractual Costs for Legacy Systems

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $6.1 million in one-time funding to meet contractual obligations associated with the  Department’s managed services platform, or Mainframe as a Service (MFaaS).

In FY 2018, the Department migrated legacy IT systems to a MFaaS solution, which eliminates the need for upfront hardware investments and provides a higher level of security.

Since FY 2018, systems have migrated to newer technology platforms, which has changed how the relatively fixed costs of the MFaaS  contract are distributed among the remaining participating divisions. Six systems remain on the mainframe.

Economic Security, Department of

This funding is intended to continue $4.0 million in one-time funding included in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget and address an increase in  the total cost of the mainframe contract. The Department is expected to utilize over $6.5 million in federal funding to cover additional  costs associated with the mainframe.

Given recent increases in the cost of the mainframe contract and the limited number of individuals who have expertise with this mainframe coding language, the most cost effective approach is to migrate the existing six systems and eliminate the contract.

The Department must maintain the mainframe contract until all systems are migrated to newer technology platforms. In an effort to eliminate the mainframe contract by FY 2030, the Executive includes funding to migrate two of the legacy systems in FY 2027.

Shifting Legacy Systems off the Mainframe

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $4.0 million in one-time funding to replace two legacy systems currently housed on the  Department’s mainframe.

The two legacy systems are the Accounts Receivable Integrated Collection System (ARICS) and the Arizona Child Care Application  Tracking System (AzCCATS). Both system replacements are expected to be completed by the end of FY 2027.

The Department must maintain the mainframe contract until all six existing systems are migrated to newer technology platforms, as there  is no viable alternative solution to support these systems. The Department has developed a multi-year plan to replace all six systems by  FY 2030, which is projected to generate annual cost savings beginning in FY 2032.

Division of Developmental Disabilities Caseload and Capitation Growth

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $298.8 million in ongoing funding for caseload adjustments for the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD) to maintain the current level of service. Included is $5.5 million in one-time funding related to an anticipated  increase in appeals.

Economic Security, Department of

DDD supports over 62,000 members who have a qualifying diagnosis or disability that causes significant limitations in daily life skills.  Adjustments are made for all three sub-populations: Arizona Long Term Care System (ALTCS), Targeted Case Management (TCM), and  State-Only.

Serving the ALTCS population within DDD is projected to cost an additional $275.8 million from the General Fund above the appropriated  levels. The population is expected to grow by 5.3%, to an average monthly population of 50,500. The capitation rate for this population is  expected to grow by 4% in the second quarter of FY 2027. The Executive anticipates that the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage  (FMAP) rate will decrease from 64.34% to 63.81% in the second quarter of FY 2027, resulting in a blended FY 2027 FMAP rate of  63.94%. Additionally, the Executive Budget incorporates an updated savings estimate based on the timeline for implementation of a new  assessment tool required by Laws 2025, Chapter 93.

The TCM population within DDD is projected to cost an additional $615,600 from the General Fund above the appropriated levels. The  population is expected to grow by 9.4% in FY 2027, to an average monthly population of 8,600. The capitation rate for this population is  projected to increase by 4% in the second quarter of FY 2027.

The State-Only population within DDD is projected to cost an additional $14.2 million from the General Fund above the appropriated  levels. The population is expected to grow by nearly 20%. Over the past three years, the costs associated with the State-Only population  have continued to exceed the appropriated level.

Additional funding increases are included to account for changes in State Funded Long Term Care (SFLTC) expenses and Medicare  Clawback payments.

The Executive estimates that an additional $673 million in Department Long-Term Care System Fund expenditure authority is needed to  support the costs of these caseload adjustments.

Economic Security, Department of

Laws 2025, Chapter 93 included several DDD reforms, such as requiring the Department to implement a new assessment tool. Due to  unforeseen delays in the implementation of the tool, the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS) has determined that  a mid-year capitation rate adjustment is needed to adequately fund DDD member costs. Education, Board of

The State Board of Education is constitutionally charged with regulating the conduct of the public school system. (g) serve as the State Board for Vocational and Technological Education; and

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Free or Reduced Price Lunch Weight

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $37 million in one-time funding to implement Laws 2022, Chapter 313.

The Free or Reduced Price Lunch (FRPL) Group B weight was introduced in FY 2023 to provide additional support to schools serving  students from working-class families.

The weight is applied to every student who qualifies for FRPL. As of FY 2025, a total student population of 667,449 qualified for FRPL,  from a total of 1,789 district and charter schools.

The FY 2026 Enacted Budget included $37 million on a one-time basis and delayed ongoing funding to FY 2028. The Executive Budget  provides continuity to the program by providing $37 million in one-time funding in FY 2027 with ongoing funding in FY 2028.

Additional Assistance

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $29 million in one-time funding to implement Laws 2022, Second Regular Session,  Chapter 313.

Increases to District Additional Assistance (DAA) and Charter Additional Assistance (CAA) were introduced in FY 2023 to strengthen  support to public schools.

Education, Department of

DAA and CAA allow public schools to continue to procure critical educational resources, including unrestricted capital or soft capital  purchases such as school transportation, technology purchases, and textbooks.

The FY 2026 Enacted Budget included $29 million on a one-time basis and delayed ongoing funding to FY 2028. The Executive Budget  provides continuity to the program by providing $29 million in one-time funding in FY 2027 with ongoing funding in FY 2028.

ESA Reform

The Executive Budget includes a decrease of $89.3 million in ongoing funding for Basic State Aid costs related to Universal Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) reform.

The Executive Budget implements an income cap that repeals prior- and future-year eligibility for universal ESA recipients whose household income is equal to or greater than $250,000.

This reform is anticipated to impact approximately 11,656 students in FY 2027.

Additionally, the Executive Budget proposes elimination of language allowing universal ESA voucher holders to carry forward unexpended ESA balances from one academic year into the next, and introduces common reporting requirements across District, Charter,  and ESA recipients.

School Meals Grants

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $3.8 million in one-time funding to continue the School Meal Grants Program at the  Department of Education.

The increased funding will reduce or eliminate the school meal co-pay for students from working families that are eligible for reducedprice meals.

Prior investments have increased access to healthy school meals for Arizona students, providing up to 10 million lunches and breakfasts  for students from working families that do not qualify for free meals and are required to pay a reduced price.

This investment covers the $0.40 co-pay for reduced-price lunches and $0.30 co-pay for reduced-price breakfasts.

Literacy Coaches

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.0 million in one-time funding to expand the Foundational Literacy Coaching Grant  program at the Department of Education.

Education, Department of

The program deploys literacy coaches to serve in eligible schools. The FY 2025 program report found that participating schools saw  measurable increases in students’ benchmark reading levels, and requests for literacy coaches from eligible schools continue to  increase.

Community College Adult Education Workforce Development Program

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $6.0 million in one-time funding to continue the Community College Adult Education Workforce Development Program.

This program provides opportunities for Arizonans to earn a high school diploma, an equivalency degree, industry-recognized credential,  or a community college degree.

This continues the one-time funding provided in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget and avoids a lapse in program services.

Continuing High School and Workforce Training Program

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1 million in one-time funding to continue the Continuing High School and Workforce  Training Program at the Department of Education.

The Continuing High School and Workforce Training Program leads to the issuance of a high school diploma and industry-recognized  credentials. The Executive Budget appropriates this funding to the Arizona Department of Education.

This continues the one-time funding provided in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget and avoids a lapse in program services.

Executive Budget Baseline Changes

Public School Enrollment Adjustment

The Executive Budget includes a decrease of $47.5 million in ongoing funding to reflect anticipated enrollment changes.

The Executive Budget projects an overall decrease of 1.38% in Average Daily Membership (ADM) in FY 2027, starting from an estimated  FY 2026 population of 1,052,826 unweighted ADM. This growth consists of a decrease of 1.54% for district schools and a decrease of  0.80% for charter schools.

Enrollment-growth costs are based on the average cost per pupil in FY 2026 for both districts and charters, adjusted for inflation.

Net Assessed Value Adjustment

Education, Department of

The Executive Budget includes a decrease of $55.2 million in ongoing funding to reflect anticipated increases in property taxes from new  construction.

The Executive Budget forecasts a 5.61% increase in Primary Net Assessed Value (NAV): 3.15% growth in existing property values and  2.47% growth from new construction.

The NAV increase for existing property does not affect the General Fund share of formula funding, as Truth in Taxation requires the  Qualifying Tax Rate (QTR) to be adjusted each year to offset changes in existing property values.

However, the increase in new construction will generate additional local property taxes that offset General Fund requirements for Basic  State Aid. The Executive projects the General Fund offset to decrease by $55.2 million.

Inflation Adjustment

The Executive Budget includes an ongoing increase of $174.1 million to account for a 2% inflation adjustment in the FY 2026 base level  amount, transportation route-mile factor, and charter school additional assistance.

The 2% inflation adjustment will add $102.27 to the FY 2026 per-pupil amount of $5,113.26, for a total of $5,215.53 in FY 2027.

Additional State Aid

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $14.8 million in ongoing funding to meet the State’s net requirements for the Homeowner’s  Rebate on residential new construction.

Adjustments are as follows:

The Homeowner’s Rebate for Tax Year 2026 will pay 50% of each homeowner’s QTR taxes, pursuant to A.R.S. § 15-972. Article IX,  Section 18 of the Arizona Constitution caps residential primary property taxes at no more than 1% of a home’s full cash value. The State  backfills any primary property tax costs for homeowners that exceed the 1% cap. The General Fund cost of this increase is $12.4 million.

Education, Department of

In FY 2026 the Enacted Budget included $531.6 million from the General Fund for Additional State Aid. Based on actual payment data,  the cost of the Homeowner's Rebate is $529.4 million, or $2.2 million less than appropriated. To account for this change, the Executive  Budget reduces in FY 2027 the base amount of funding for Additional State Aid by $2.2 million.

Laws 2022, Second Regular Session, Chapter 171 reduces the assessment ratio for commercial properties, which continues to phase-in  in FY 2027 and is anticipated to have an additional cost of $4.6 million.

Basic State Aid - Base Adjustment

The Executive Budget includes a decrease of $26.6 million in ongoing funding to rebase net annual funding for anticipated enrollment  and other changes.

The FY 2026 Enacted Budget included estimates for FY 2025 Basic State Aid Formula Base Adjustments, which revised funding  amounts for School District Equalization, Charter Equalization, and ESA costs to $7.197 billion, $2.114 billion, and $1.002 billion, respectively. However, actual ending year costs for these items were $51.5 million lower, $35.9 million lower, and $62.7 million higher.

The Executive Budget responds to these factors by proposing a rebase in annual funding for anticipated enrollment and other changes.  In an effort to rebase student population forecasts and, effectively, Basic State Aid appropriation levels, the Executive estimate for population growth in FY 2027 begins with 1,052,826 unweighted ADM for FY 2026.

ESA Growth

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $156.5 million in ongoing funding for Basic State Aid costs related to Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) program growth.

The Executive Budget projects an increase of 7,954 Universal and 2,558 Pre-Universal ESA vouchers in FY 2027, increasing total  program enrollment to over 111,000 students.

Department of Emergency and Military Affairs

Emergency and Military Affairs, Department of

The Arizona Department of Emergency and Military Affairs (DEMA) is administered and controlled by the Governor and headed by The  Adjutant General as Military Chief of Staff and agency Director.

The Department consists of the Army National Guard, Air National Guard, Joint Task Force-AZ, Division of Emergency Management,  and Division of Administrative Services. Collectively these components provide military and emergency management capabilities and  services to the citizens of Arizona in three distinct levels: community, state, and federal.

These components utilize state and federal resources to perform homeland defense and emergency management activities to protect  the citizens of Arizona, provide trained military units in support of civil authorities for domestic emergencies, and support federal  combatant commanders for national defense and homeland security missions.

Link to the AGENCY’S WEBSITE:    https://dema.az.gov/

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Grant Support Staff

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $472,600 in ongoing funding for 5.0 FTE positions to continue one-time funding provided  in the FY 2026 Enacted Budget for additional grant support staff in the DEMA Emergency Management Division.

With the additional positions, DEMA originally projected a reduction in the average time to process reimbursements from 14 months to  4.5 months by June 2029, or roughly a 25% decrease in processing time each year. As of the second quarter of FY 2026, DEMA had  surpassed its goal for the year by reducing average processing time to nine months, equating to a 40% reduction in less than one year.

Continued investment in these positions is necessary for DEMA to reach its revised goals to reduce processing time, fully resolve the  multi-year backlog by June 2027, and sufficiently fulfill its statutory duties. These positions will also provide DEMA with the additional  capacity necessary for processing new federal reimbursements.

Expand Counter Drug Task Force

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $2.0 million in one-time funding to expand the Arizona National Guard Counter Drug Task  Force (CDTF).

The CDTF will expand on its efforts to curtail drug trafficking activities throughout the State, detect drone activity related to drug smuggling, address threats posted by transnational criminal organizations, and continue to partner with local law enforcement through Task  Force SAFE.

Governor's Emergency Fund Deposit

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $20.0 million in one-time funding to the aggregate amount of liabilities cap incurred under  a declaration of disaster to account for new payment practices from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

FEMA has become both stricter and slower in approving payments for disasters. FEMA denied Arizona’s request for a Major Disaster  Declaration for the September 25–27, 2025, Gila and Mohave County Flooding, despite the fact that preliminary assessments document  damages that far exceed appropriate thresholds. This funding will ensure that the State is able to continue supporting localities that are  negatively affected by major disasters, despite decreased reliability and funding from the federal government in times of emergency.

The Executive Budget includes a proposed Legislative change to raise the Governor’s Emergency Fund expenditure cap. The proposed  language can be found in the Executive Budget Legislative Changes section.

text:
Environmental Quality, Department of

The Arizona Legislature established the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) as the state’s environmental regulatory  agency under the Environmental Quality Act of 1986 to serve as a separate, cabinet-level agency to administer all of Arizona’s environmental protection programs.

Link to the AGENCY’S WEBSITE:    https://azdeq.gov/

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Fund Consolidation: Recycling Fund and Solid Waste Fee Fund

The Executive Budget includes consolidating the Recycling Fund into the Solid Waste Fee Fund (SWFF).

Since the establishment of fees for the Solid Waste Program in FY 2012, SWFF revenue has not been sufficient to cover annual expenditures. The Department has mitigated this issue every year by utilizing the Recycling Fund.

The fund consolidation continues the critical work of both the Recycling Grant Program and the Solid Waste Program, while streamlining  administrative processes. This aligns with current uses of the Recycling Fund and improves future fund capacity, allowing both programs  to deliver more programming in future years.

The proposed statutory change for the fund consolidation can be found in the Executive Budget Legislative Changes section.

Investment in Geothermal Energy

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $1.5 million in one-time funding to invest in research on the potential of geothermal  energy.

The funding provides the state match to draw down $1.0 million in State Energy Program federal funding, for a total investment of $2.5  million.

Arizona has significant geothermal resources that could be utilized to expand the state's energy portfolio. Research into the State's  geothermal resources will reduce the initial barriers and costs for private development of geothermal projects that generate affordable  power and quality jobs.

The funding will be transferred to the Arizona Geological Survey and used for data collection, analysis, and management.

Emissions Inspection Contract Increases

Environmental Quality, Department of

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $3.1 million in ongoing funding to cover anticipated increases in contract expenses for the  State's emissions inspection program.

The Department utilizes a private vendor for emissions inspection tests. The contract with the vendor was renegotiated with an effective  date starting in FY 2027 through FY 2028. The new contract stipulates rate increases to ADEQ for the tests performed by the vendor.

The funding will allow the Department to fully operate the state emissions inspection program under the renewed contract.

Water Quality Fee Fund Deposit

The Executive Budget includes an ongoing deposit of $9.5 million from the General Fund into the Water Quality Fee Fund (WQFF).

The WQFF supports surface water, groundwater, and drinking water programs that protect the quality of the state’s water. Functions  supported include water monitoring, permit issuance, and water quality inspections to enforce water quality standards.

The Fund has historically had - and continues to have - insufficient revenue to cover annual expenditures. In FY 2024, the Department  increased fees. However, the fees set do not meet annual expenditures, due to adverse effects on fee payers. In recent years, the cash  shortfall has been addressed by one-time deposits.

This ongoing deposit will provide a permanent solution to address the cash shortfall.

CERCLA State Assurance Cost

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $4.9 million in one-time non-lapsing funding to pay for the entire State's share of the  Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) cleanup for the Iron King Mine - Humboldt Smelter  Superfund site.

The site, located in central Arizona near Dewey-Humboldt, contains hazardous waste from two independent facilities that left behind high  levels of arsenic, lead, and other metals. In 2023, the EPA issued a Record of Decision for the site, finalizing the remedy and estimated  cost.

Environmental Quality, Department of

The remedy will include, among other remedial actions, excavations and containment of the hazardous waste at on-site repositories.

As part of the contract, the State is obligated to pay 10% of the total cleanup costs. The contract outlines that ADEQ is required to make  three payments of at least $2.0 million every 12 months for a total of $8.3 million. The funding will complete the State's payment obligations.

Voluntary Vehicle Repair Program Support

The Executive Budget includes a one-time deposit of $2.2 million from the Air Quality Fee Fund into the Voluntary Vehicle Repair  Program (VVRP) Fund.

The deposit will support the demand for the program, which assists working class individuals and families with the cost of emissionsrelated vehicle repairs after a failed emissions test.

Laws 2021, Chapter 27 expanded eligibility for the program. This has increased the program’s popularity, as evidenced by an increase in  participation from 1,632 vehicles repaired in FY 2021 to 3,735 in FY 2023. Funding for the program has not kept pace with the demand,  resulting in the Department limiting participation to a first-come first-served basis in FY 2024. The FY 2025 Enacted Budget included $2.9  million to support the program.

This funding will ensure that the Department is able to continue to meet the demand in FY 2027.

H. R. 1 Impacts on Air Quality

The Executive Budget includes an ongoing deposit of $3.9 million from the General Fund into the Air Quality Fund to backfill federal  funding that supports air quality activities performed by ADEQ.

The Clean Air Act regulates air pollution from all sources, setting national standards for air quality, and controlling hazardous emissions.

H.R.1 rescinds Clean Air Act Section 103 and Section 105 Grants. Without Section 103 and Section 105 grant funding, ADEQ’s Air  Quality Division will lose about 26% of its current operating funding.

Environmental Quality, Department of

The loss of federal funding will result in reduced air quality monitoring, planning, forecasting, compliance inspections, and data management activities.

As a result, many Arizonans could experience health impacts such as increased cases and severity of asthma, respiratory irritation, and  lung disease from breathing poorer air quality. In addition, businesses may experience greater delays and costs, as ADEQ will lose  funding that supports timely delivery of required permits and activities that support industry compliance.

The Executive Budget aligns with current law by restoring this funding from a portion of the Corporate Income Tax revenue.

Equalization, Board of

The State Board of Equalization provides an independent appeal process for taxpayers, county assessors, and the Arizona Department  of Revenue in disputes relating to the valuation and classification of property in the State. The Board is comprised of 41 members: 21  (including the chairman) appointed by the Governor and 10 each from Maricopa and Pima counties (appointed by the boards of supervisors of those counties). Under A.R.S. § 42-14001 et al., the Board’s authority extends to centrally assessed property statewide. By statute,  the Board also can provide hearing officer services for outlying counties; currently, the Board provides services to Cochise, Mohave,  Pinal, Santa Cruz, and Yavapai counties.

Board of Executive Clemency

Executive Clemency, Board of

The Board of Executive Clemency is a five-member board appointed by the Governor and is statutorily empowered to make decisions  regarding:

(a) discretionary release of those inmates who are eligible for parole and/or home arrest (inmates whose crimes were committed on or  before December 31, 1993);

(b) revocation of parole (or community supervision for crimes committed on or after January 1, 1994) for offenders found to be in violation  of the terms and conditions of their release;

(c) absolute discharge from parole; and

(d) modification of release conditions and release rescissions.

The Board also makes clemency recommendations to the Governor on requests for commutation of sentence, including death penalty  sentences, reprieves in matters related to death penalty cases, and pardons.

Link to the AGENCY’S WEBSITE:    https://boec.az.gov/

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Critical Board Membership Recruitment

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $156,700 in ongoing funding for Board member salaries to support recruitment and retention of qualified individuals and be more competitive with market compensation.

Retention is vital to mitigate increased caseload. The Board is anticipated to have only two confirmed members at the start of the 2026  Legislative session, due to member retirements and unconfirmed candidates reaching the end of their allowable term of service.

When caseloads per member increase, Board members must work longer hours to process cases timely and within statutory timeframes.  If one Board member is missing, the caseload increases by 25.3% for each remaining Board member, which adds to the significant  increase in caseload the Board has already experienced in recent years.

Since 2023, commutation cases have increased by 124.0%, revocation cases have increased by 77.0%, and probable-cause cases have  increased by 65.0%.

In partnership with local, county, state and federal agencies, the Arizona Department of Forestry and Fire Management (DFFM) protects  Arizona’s people by: providing coordination and resource response for the suppression and management of wildland fire; delivering  education to aid in wildland fire prevention; providing integrated management strategies, technical assistance and information through  various Department programs; collaborating in forest restoration projects; and ensuring fire and life safety through permitting, plan  reviews and building inspections.

Link to the AGENCY’S WEBSITE:    https://dffm.az.gov/about

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Wildfire Suppression Funding

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $20.0 million in one-time funding for wildfire suppression.

Arizona wildland firefighting costs have been much higher in recent years compared to the average $5.8 million in costs for fiscal years  2010 through 2020. The rise in wildland firefighting costs is not isolated to Arizona, as the western U.S. is experiencing drier, warmer  climates, with forests that have not been adequately maintained, resulting in an increase in State spending on multi-jurisdictional wildfires. In FY 2025, Arizonans experienced a total of 1,701 wildfires that burned 245,700 acres.

The Department has received intermittent infusions of funding that have not kept pace with spending.

Remove One-Time FY 2026 Appropriation(s)

The Executive Budget removes in FY 2027 the following one-time FY 2026 appropriation(s):

- Northern Arizona Wildland Fire Training Facility: $4,000,000

The Executive Budget aligns with current law by backing out the appropriation(s).

Gaming, Department of

The Arizona Department of Gaming (ADG) regulates tribal gaming, event wagering, fantasy sports, horse racing and pari-mutuel/simulcast wagering, and unarmed combat sports; investigates illegal off-reservation activities; and provides and supports prevention, education, and treatment programs for people and families affected by problem gambling through its Division of Problem Gambling (DPG).

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Fund Consolidation: Event Wagering Fund, Fantasy Sports Contest Fund, and Unarmed Combat Subaccount

The Executive Budget consolidates the Fantasy Sports Contest Fund and the Unarmed Combat Subaccount into the Event Wagering  Fund.

The restructuring is intended to enhance operational efficiencies, resolve current financial impediments, and reduce the administrative  burden.

Under the new structure, the Department will be better positioned to support Arizona’s event wagering industries.

Preserving Racing's Regulatory Capacity

The Executive Budget returns to the Department the authority to adjust the Regulatory Wagering Assessment (RWA).

The RWA is currently capped in statute at 0.5%. Due to this cap and increased HISA cost assessed by the federal government, the  Department does not have sufficient resources to regulate horseracing.

In order to meet the additional regulatory need, the Department intends to revert the RWA to the level currently set in rule, which is 0.75%  in May-June and 0.85% in October-April. Should the RWA continue to be capped at 0.5%, the Department would need General Fund  monies to continue the regulatory duties prescribed to the Division of Racing.

The Executive Budget includes a proposed Legislative change to increase the RWA statutory cap. The proposed language can e found  in the Executive Budget Legislative changes section.

Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Newborn Screening - DMD

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $754,900 in ongoing funding and 2.0 FTE positions to add Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy  (DMD) to the Arizona newborn screening panel.

DMD is a genetic disorder characterized by the progressive loss of muscle. It is a multi-systemic condition that affects many parts of the  body and results in deterioration of the skeletal, heart, and lung muscles.

Laws 2025, Chapter 239 requires DMD to be added to the Arizona newborn screening panel by October 2027.

Extreme Heat Mitigation

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $10.0 million in one-time funding to provide investments to mitigate the public health  effects of heat.

- $4.2 million for Cooling Centers and Heat Relief

This will fund items such as retrofitting storage units into Cooltainers, providing essential heat supplies, and operational costs of mobile  and grant funded cooling centers.

- $3.7 million for Heat Relief Training

This will fund items such as training for EMS personnel, expand training and compliance efforts surrounding heat issues for workers, and  training and outreach to encourage adoption of the most recent International Building Codes for safer and more insulated buildings.

- $1.5 million for Call Center Operations

Contract to establish a statewide heat call center that serves as a vital, non-profit-like information and referral service during the extreme  heat season.

- $500,000 for Critical Transportation Services

Providing rideshare services.

Prescott Historical Society

Historical Society, Prescott

The Prescott Historical Society operates the Sharlot Hall Museum, which was founded in 1928 and is located on the grounds of the first  territorial Governor's residence and offices. The nearly four-acre landscaped campus features 11 exhibit buildings, including four  restored historic structures: the territorial Governor's Mansion (1864), Fort Misery (1864), the Fremont House (1875), and the Victorianera Bashford House (1877). The Lawler Exhibit Center (1977) hosts both permanent and changing exhibits, an historic theater, and  storage of extensive historic and prehistoric objects. A large Archive Library (2008) houses a 10,000 book library and hundreds of thousands of images, documents, maps and oral histories.

In March 2013, a new support facility constructed with non-State funds was completed. In April 2014, a new admissions building, also  privately financed, was added. A 10,000 square foot Education Center, financed entirely by the non-profit Sharlot Hall Historical Society,  was completed in the summer of 2020. The Bob Stump VA Medical Center hosts a branch museum that interprets the history of Fort  Whipple. Public programs include the annual Prescott Indian Art Market, Frontier Christmas, musical and theatrical historical productions, living history interpretations in both indoor and outdoor settings, heritage gardens, arboretum, lecture series, education tours, and  outreach opportunities for children and adults.

Homeland Security, Department of

The Department administers federal grants to State and local agencies to protect our border and prevent or reduce Arizona’s vulnerability to terrorist attacks, as well as driving best-in-class, enterprise cybersecurity solutions in an effort to ensure the protection of all  government functions within the State of Arizona. Agency Budget Summary

Major Executive Budget Initiatives and Funding

Border Coordination Office

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $765,000 in ongoing funding and 4.0 FTE position authority to continue the operations of  the Border Coordination Office (BCO).

Established in FY 2024 using American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) dollars, the BCO’s purposes include the following:

- Serve as the central point of coordination for State activities related to border security and safety;

- Monitor border operations; coordinate the State’s response to situations along the southern border and across the state;

- Coordinate engagements with local leaders and community partners;

- Build and maintain relationships with local governments and law enforcement agencies at the federal, State, county, and local levels;

- Make recommendations to improve border operations;

Funding will cover the costs of 4.0 FTE positions and operational needs of the Office.

Repurpose Statewide Cybersecurity Grants

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $10.0 million in one-time funding to provide cybersecurity tools as well as technical expertise and support to public sector organizations and State agencies.

In addition, the Executive Budget eliminates the Statewide Cybersecurity Grants SLI, creates a new Cyber Ready Arizona SLI, and shifts  the Statewide Cybersecurity Grants SLI funding of $10.0 million to the new Cyber Ready Arizona SLI.

Homeland Security, Department of

The Cyber Ready Arizona SLI will provide the necessary support for the State and local entities to preserve and protect digital environments from bad actors. Without this program, governmental organizations lacking in-house cybersecurity expertise and tools will be left  vulnerable to the growing threat of cybersecurity attacks and data breaches.

Multi-Factor Authentication Implementation Costs

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $550,000 in ongoing funding and $300,000 in one-time funding to support the costs of fully  implementing and maintaining multi-factor authentication (MFA) for the State's financial and human resources system, AZ360.

AZ360 was launched in FY 2025 by the Department of Administration. The ongoing funding for this initiative enables the Department of  Homeland Security to continue administering MFA for AZ360. MFA ensures that State employee information remains safe and secure.

The one-time costs are associated with deploying physical tokens for State agencies that are unable to use mobile or app-based MFA for  the AZ360 system. Tokens are devices that provide generated one-time passwords that are used as an additional factor for logging in.

The Executive Budget includes an increase of $10.5 million in ongoing funding for Adult Probation and Juvenile Probation Officer salaries  and employee-related expenses.
